title: Heat waves are getting so bad that even this cactus can't survive
summary: Despite evolving for millennia to thrive in the blazing Sonoran Desert, the iconic saguaro cactus is struggling to survive escalating heat waves.

image.caption: Desert Botanical Garden lab manager Ali Schuessler gathers data on saguaro cacti at South Mountain Park and Preserve in Phoenix, Ariz., on July 14, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)

blocks.text: Science
Despite evolving for millennia to thrive in the blazing Sonoran Desert, the iconic saguaro cactus is struggling to survive escalating heat waves.
Nighttime temperatures mess with cactus's key adaptation, hotter El Niños kill baby cacti
The cactus seen in countless Hollywood westerns and on Arizona licence plates can tower 40 feet (12 metres) or higher and live 150 years or more.

Before 2020, about one to two per cent of saguaro cacti died each year, according to researchers at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix, one of the hottest zones in saguaro country. But as stretches of extreme heat buffeted Arizona, the mortality rate in the city that researchers attribute just to heat rose to four per cent in 2021. And then to seven per cent in 2023.
The heat-related death rate has since recovered, said the Botanical Garden’s research director Kevin Hultine, but only to four per cent, leaving him worried about the viability of the iconic cactus.

Heat waves were once relatively small, intermittent episodes 6 ½ decades ago. With climate change, they've grown into supersized, long-lasting and globe-spanning weather events that Reuters has dubbed "heat storms."
A dead saguaro cactus lays near a healthy one at South Mountain Park and Preserve in Phoenix on July 20, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)

The sustained heat can enfeeble the cactus in many ways — by damaging its skin, which can impair the plant’s food production and expose it to infection, or by evaporating away its water, causing it to sag and collapse.
Among the changes of recent decades is that nocturnal heat storms now often blanket the desert.

The saguaro and other cacti and succulents evolved to conduct a critical photosynthesis step not in the dangerous heat of the day but in the protective cool of the night. At daybreak, the saguaro’s tough outer skin tightens its pores, known as stomata, massively restricting evaporation during the hot day.

But with its pores constricted, the saguaro can absorb hardly any carbon dioxide, hindering its ability to generate nutrients. So, it waits for ​sundown. As temperatures fall at night, the cactus opens its microscopic pores, taking deep drafts of vital carbon dioxide.

Then, enzymes transform the carbon dioxide into a form that the cactus can store until sunrise. At dawn, different enzymes release the stored CO2, allowing the rest of the photosynthesis process to turn it into food.
But there’s a catch. Nocturnal heat can disrupt the work of the nighttime enzymes.
Effectively, a hot night can deprive the saguaro of its daily bread.
A close-up of the ribs of a dead saguaro cactus at South Mountain Park and Preserve in Phoenix, Ariz., on July 20, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)
What’s more, hot nights can also evaporate more of the saguaro’s internal water.

It’s the damage from such intense heat that researcher Ali Schuessler studies on the saguaro that grow not far away on South Mountain Park and Preserve, a hilly area overlooking the city. If the temperatures stay hot enough for long enough, saguaros can lose much of their internal water to evaporation. The saguaro needs its internal water to stay rigid, so too much water loss can cause the cactus to buckle and ⁠topple.

"I’ll never forget how shocked I was the first time one of them fell over, and our horticulture team was cutting it up and feeling the inside of the plant, and how hot it was," she recalled. The saguaro was as hot as "your tea or your coffee."
'A relic'
The saguaro’s fate is likely to unfold across decades, because it is a slow species. It grows slowly; it can live as long as 200 years, though 150 is more common; and it reproduces very slowly.

While an adult saguaro can hold a thousand gallons of water, a ​year-old saguaro is only about a quarter inch tall (two-thirds of a centimetre). This means the summer heat can kill it by simply drying it out.
How these illegal, endangered cacti ended up at Montreal’s Botanical Garden
In the northern Sonoran Desert, El Niño often provides something critical for baby saguaros: plentiful winter rains that allow the cactus to soak up enough water to survive the brutal summer.

But the last El Niño to bring along a cactus baby boom was a "super" El Niño in 1982-83. Since then, says research director Hultine, El Niños have often sent heavy rains, but they have also been accompanied by more heat storms and heat waves.
Schuessler fears for the saguaro’s long-term viability: "Even if these guys can exist out on the landscape for a long period of time, ⁠if they can’t reproduce, then they’re done for."
Today, another super El Niño to rival the one from the 1980s has formed over the Pacific. But because of the increasing heat storms and heat waves, Hultine is not hopeful.
The area’s saguaros, he says, are "effectively a relic."
